content: The emergence of Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) antigen-based skin tests (TBSTs) has highlighted the need for alternative diagnostic tools for tuberculosis (TB) infection. These newer TBSTs utilize specific antigens, such as ESAT-6 and CFP-10, and combine the simplicity of skin test platforms with the specificity of interferon-gamma release assays (IGRAs). Examples of these tests include Cy-Tb (Serum Institute of India, India), Diaskintest® (Generium, Russian Federation), and C-TST (formerly known as the ESAT-6-CFP-10 test, Anhui Zhifei Longcom, China). These tests involve intradermal injection of antigens and are read after 48–72 hours by measuring the induration in millimeters, following the Mantoux method. Emerging evidence suggests that TBSTs may have diagnostic specificity comparable to IGRAs and may provide more reliable results in children, adolescents, and people living with HIV (PLHIV) compared to the traditional tuberculin skin test (TST). However, this evidence has not been systematically reviewed. The World Health Organization (WHO) has shifted its assessment process for TB diagnostics to focus on evaluating classes of technologies rather than specific products. Key factors guiding implementation include diagnostic accuracy, epidemiological and geographical settings, operational aspects (e.g., turnaround times, throughput, infrastructure), economic considerations, and qualitative aspects such as acceptability, equity, and end-user preferences. The TBST class is defined as in vivo skin tests for detecting TB infection using Mtb-specific antigens (ESAT-6 and CFP-10). In 2021, WHO commissioned a systematic review of published and unpublished data on this new class of tests, which had not been previously reviewed. The review included data on diagnostic accuracy, safety, economic aspects, and qualitative evidence on feasibility, acceptability, equity, and end-user values. A Guideline Development Group (GDG) convened by WHO in early 2022 evaluated the findings and made recommendations on these diagnostic technologies. The evaluated technologies included Cy-Tb, Diaskintest, and C-TST. Current recommendations are based on the evaluation of data for these tests, and findings cannot be extrapolated to other brand-specific tests. Any new in-class technologies will require specific evaluation by WHO. The updated policy is incorporated into the WHO TB Knowledge Sharing Platform, an online resource for global TB policies. The GDG concluded that the diagnostic accuracy of TBSTs is similar to IGRAs and superior to TST. However, concerns were raised about the certainty of evidence in many areas and the lack of longitudinal studies assessing the impact on TB outcomes. The risk of bias was primarily due to non-blinded studies, and the quality of evidence varied among the different tests. For Diaskintest and C-TST, specificity data were generated in high TB burden settings, and additional analysis considered concordance with WHO-recommended IGRAs. No safety concerns were identified for the class of tests, but regulatory approval by competent agencies is essential before their introduction. Limited data on cost and cost-effectiveness were available. Modeling calibrated to Brazil, South Africa, and the United Kingdom suggested that TBSTs would be cost-saving compared to TST and IGRAs in Brazil and South Africa, and cost-saving compared to TST but only cost-effective compared to IGRAs in the UK. Qualitative evidence indicates that TBSTs are likely to improve health equity by providing a more accurate, low-cost test for resource-limited settings where TST is already in use. TBSTs were perceived to have greater accuracy than TST and were considered desirable because they avoid the negative consequences of false-positive results. The feasibility of using TBSTs in settings where TST is already in use was supported by the existing infrastructure and training. All three evaluated TBSTs (Cy-Tb, Diaskintest, and C-TST) have the potential to be used for detecting TB infection and are recommended. The GDG supported extrapolation of the recommendation to subpopulations such as PLHIV, children and adolescents under 18 years, and individuals vaccinated with Bacille Calmette-Guérin (BCG). Testing for TB infection is not a prerequisite for initiating TB preventive treatment (TPT) in children under five years who are household contacts of people with active TB, but testing increases the certainty of benefit from TPT. The evaluated TBSTs use intradermal injection of ESAT-6 and CFP-10 antigens, which stimulate a T-cell immune response and induce a specific skin reaction in individuals with TB infection. The immune response is measured as induration in millimeters after 48–72 hours. Cy-Tb is produced by the Serum Institute of India, Diaskintest is a recombinant protein produced by genetically modified Escherichia coli, and C-TST uses a recombinant fusion protein of ESAT-6 and CFP-10. These products are approved by their respective national regulatory authorities. In 2021, WHO commissioned a systematic review of data on the new class of TBSTs, focusing on diagnostic accuracy, safety, economic aspects, and qualitative evidence. The overarching policy question was whether TBSTs should be used as an alternative to TST or IGRAs to identify individuals at risk of progressing from TB infection to TB disease. Evidence synthesis was structured around diagnostic accuracy, safety, cost-effectiveness, and user perspectives. The GRADE approach was used to assess the quality of evidence, which was rated as high, moderate, low, or very low based on factors such as risk of bias, indirectness, inconsistency, imprecision, and other considerations. The systematic review identified studies evaluating the sensitivity, specificity, and concordance of TBSTs. Sensitivity data were derived from 20 studies involving 1,627 participants with microbiologically confirmed TB. Specificity data were generated in low TB burden populations. The quality of evidence was systematically assessed, and findings were summarized in GRADE profiles.
